lesson.subtitle: Lesson 25 -- The Difficult Stakeholder
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Flávio Masaharu Kuroda | Lesson 25 -- The Difficult Stakeholder
lesson.grammar_point: polite disagreement (I see your point, but; I'm not sure I agree; with respect; I take your point)

listenings.text: Every big deal has one person who can say no, and it is rarely the person you talk to every week. Most salespeople make one of two mistakes with that person. Some try to go around them, straight to the CEO. That almost never works, and the skeptic remembers it. Others argue: they answer every concern with an opinion. My advice is different. First, ask for the concern in their own words, and say it back to them. Second, disagree with data, never with your feelings. With respect, our numbers show something different. Third, give them something to win, so they can say yes without losing face. Most skeptics are not against you. They are risk-averse, and they are protecting their company.

I am the person salespeople call difficult. When a project reaches my desk, my job is to find what can go wrong, so I disagree a lot, and I do it on purpose. I want to see what the supplier does next. Last year, two suppliers were in the final round. The first one listened, said I take your point about the risk, and came back two days later with a reference I could call. The second one did not like my questions, so he called our CEO and asked him to overrule me. The CEO forwarded his email to me. That was the end of the conversation. I have a veto in every deal above a certain size, and I use it on people who do not respect the process.
